column1: - Custom instructions (Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, CLAUDE.md, and similar) steer AI code assistants toward secure output · - Developers remain accountable for generated code; AI output requires the same review, test, and SAST discipline as human-written code · - Instructions should stay concise and project-specific; irrelevant security text increases wrong or over-fit code · - Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) loops ask the assistant to review and fix its own prior output with linters and scanners
column2: - Instructions do not replace ASVS, SCVS, or AISVS verification; they reduce common assistant mistakes only · - Persona prompts like act as a security expert often degrade results in cited experiments · - Assistant-suggested dependencies may be hallucinated or outdated; pin versions and verify packages
column3: - Encode input validation, output encoding, secrets handling, and least-privilege defaults in project instruction files · - Require parameterized queries, constant-time comparisons for secrets, and secure error handling without leaking internals · - Mandate SBOM generation, dependency scanning, and CI SAST/DAST in generated pipeline snippets · - Add language-specific rules (bounds-checked C, no shell=True in Python subprocess, pinned container digests with cosign verification)

column1: - Agent security spans model, system guardrails, harness orchestration, and tool access; each layer needs distinct controls · - Primary attack vectors: prompt injection, memory poisoning, and tool supply-chain compromise where tool output re-enters reasoning · - Misaligned benign requests can cause harm without an external attacker when scope and permissions are too broad · - Shared responsibility across developers, deployers, tool providers, third-party surfaces, and users who grant authority
column2: - Probabilistic model defenses alone cannot guarantee safety; deterministic limits on tools and egress must sit outside the reasoning loop · - Persistent memory propagates poisoned state across turns and agents; harness logging is the enforcement and audit point · - MCP and similar protocols do not guarantee secure implementations; discipline at integration time determines exposure
column3: - Apply least privilege on tools, filesystem, network egress, and credentials; sandbox execution environments · - Block the lethal trifecta: do not combine private-data access, untrusted content, and external communication in one agent without mitigations · - Require human confirmation before irreversible or high-stakes actions; adapt oversight for multi-agent parallel workflows · - Vet tools in directories or sandboxes; combine instruction hierarchies, classifiers, and provenance-aware interpreters such as CaMeL where feasible

column1: - Maps how frontier AI safety frameworks set cyber capability thresholds, assess models, and deploy mitigations · - Dual-use cyber capabilities help defenders patch and detect while lowering barriers for offensive misuse · - Emerging consensus thresholds: non-expert uplift for sophisticated attacks and end-to-end autonomous cyber operations · - Zero-day discovery and attacks against hardened targets are explicit escalation markers across member frameworks
column2: - Threshold wording (significant, meaningful, material uplift) remains subjective; cross-vendor comparability is incomplete · - Benchmarks saturate and suffer contamination; CTF and cyber-range scores may reflect training exposure not operational risk · - Defender benefit from the same model capabilities must weigh into release decisions, not offense alone
column3: - Threat-model AI-cyber paths with ATT&CK, Cyber Kill Chain, and STRIDE; update models as incidents and assessments arrive · - Run tiered capability assessments: knowledge benchmarks, agent CTF/cyber-range tasks, safeguard evals, and expert red teams · - Tie assessment results to output policies, refusals, and monitoring for vulnerability-query and exploit-development patterns · - Document assumptions on actor skill, target hardening, and autonomy before crossing published capability thresholds

column1: - Tailored checklists for model capability tier (frontier vs general purpose) crossed with release type (restricted API, closed, open) · - Covers R&D risk scanning, pre-deployment safeguards, post-deployment monitoring, and decommission paths · - Expanded 2024 guidance assigns obligations across adapters, hosting services, and application developers in open-model chains · - Significant capability updates after deployment trigger renewed governance, not one-time sign-off
column2: - Voluntary guidance meant to complement regulation such as EU GPAI Code of Practice, not replace legal duties · - Third-party audit methods and incident-reporting baselines remain immature across the industry · - Research or limited releases may warrant lighter oversight than wide public deployment of frontier models
column3: - Select the checklist matching model capability and release type on the Model Deployment Guidance site · - Implement access controls, rate limits, terms of use, and architecture-embedded safety before external release · - Monitor for misuse, jailbreaks, and downstream impacts; define restrict, suspend, and retire criteria · - Publish model cards and downstream safety tooling for open releases; distribute responsibility across the value chain

column1: - Voluntary Singapore framework for deploying agents built in-house or via third-party platforms · - Four dimensions: assess and bound risks upfront, meaningful human accountability, technical lifecycle controls, end-user responsibility · - Agent components include model, instructions, memory, planning, tools, protocols, access controls, guardrails, approvals, and logging · - v1.5 adds multi-agent and third-party agent risks, automation bias practices, and operational case studies
column2: - Continuous human approval for every agent step does not scale; define checkpoints for high-stakes and irreversible actions only · - Multi-agent architectures diffuse accountability unless roles are mapped across the agentic value chain · - Protocols (MCP, A2A, commerce protocols) evolve quickly; controls must track new tool and agent interaction surfaces
column3: - Bound action-space up front: limit tools, permissions, reversibility, and autonomy per use case · - Assign responsibilities across platform providers, system integrators, and app developers before deployment · - Test agents for execution accuracy, policy adherence, and tool use pre-release; monitor continuously post-release · - Disclose agent scope to users; train operators to resist automation bias and maintain override and audit trails · - Validate alignment with AI Verify toolkit and ISO/IEC 42001 crosswalk where attestations are required
